Autoresearch

You already run Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse. Point any of them at a problem and they'll keep improving it while you sleep.

The idea comes from Karpathy's autoresearch: one constraint, one mechanical metric, one loop that iterates on its own. The gains compound.

Set the GOAL. The agent runs the LOOP. You wake up to results. You don't need AGI for this. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that never quits.

The core skill, bundled runtime, installation, and verification surface all support Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse. Hook guardrails ship for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

What happens when the metric stalls? Fork-and-flush. The way Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447) escape plateaus. At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas (randomness). The other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). In Guided mode, R sets the split. When the orchestrator hits a plateau, it answers with FORK before it gives up. Details in guide/autoresearch.md.

Bumblebee is a read-only inventory collector for package, extension, and developer-tool metadata on macOS and Linux developer endpoints.

It answers one supply-chain question: an advisory names a package, extension, or version, so which developer machines show a match in their on-disk metadata right now?

SBOMs tell you what shipped. EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. Supply-chain response often needs a different view: messy local state across lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee turns that scattered on-disk state into structured NDJSON component records. Hand it an exposure catalog and it flags exact matches, so you can run a fast, read-only exposure check when you already know what you're looking for.

SkillsBench tests whether AI agents can actually use Skills to complete professional work across different domains. The point is to measure how much better a model solves complex real-world tasks when it has specialized Skills on hand.

The original setup hands each task the one specialized Skill it needs. That's not how production works, so we built a harder version: every task runs in a global environment with all 195 specialized Skills installed, and nothing else changes. The agent has to find the right Skills, pick them out, and string them into a workflow that gets the job done.

We ran vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench with DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline setup. Against the baseline without vibeskills, the mean verifier reward went up 21.12 percentage points, token consumption dropped 29.6%, and tool calls fell 33.1%.

Semantic version control built on Git.

Instead of lines changed, sem tells you what entities changed: functions, methods, classes.

Releases

sem is a semantic version control tool that works on top of Git. It parses your code with tree-sitter, extracts every function, class, and method as an entity, and diffs at the entity level instead of lines. So you see "function blahh was modified" instead of "lines x-y changed."

It works in any Git repo with no setup.

If you're on macOS 0.7.0 or earlier, don't use the in-app updater. Update by hand.

Two things break in those versions. The updater can quit the app and never relaunch it when a macOS system update is waiting to install. And it hands Apple Silicon Macs the Intel build.

Both are fixed from 0.7.2 onward. But getting to 0.7.2 takes a manual step: download the DMG from the 0.7.2 release, grab the arm64 file if you're on Apple Silicon or the plain .dmg on Intel, then drag SkillsGate to Applications.

Your settings, favorites, and installed skills are kept. After that, updates install normally.
